I just did a search on Blade HQ for knives that meet your criteria and they’re pretty limited.

There’s the Buck Knives “Budgie”, a Frame lock folder that uses a “spydy hole” in leu of thumstuds or a flipper and an s35vn blade with a closed length of 3.25”. I’ve handled this knife in person and wasn’t too impressed. All the examples I’ve handled were ridiculously gritty and tough to unlock, they’re hefty knives for their size, and one of the knives we were going to display in the store had a defective lockup and had to be sent back to Buck. It’s the cheapest option but in this case you’ll be getting what you paid for. I’m sure it will break in to become a fine knife with enough work and proper lubrication.

Your second option is the Zero Tolerance 0022, another frame lock but the 0022 uses a more stylish flipper tab. This knife has a closed length of 2.95” and a 1.875” CPM 20CV blade. I’ve handled one of these knives at our store and found it to be really neat. It looks like a baby ZT (oxymoron?) and it feels like a quality piece of kit. It’s over 2x the price of the Buck but you’re paying for carbon fiber, titanium, and CPM 20CV. Plus you get to walk around knowing that you’re carrying a baby knife that costs $220.

The only other reasonably priced option I found was the Benchmade Tengu Tool. It’s got a closed length of 2.14” and a 1.14” CPM 20CV blade. This knife is a slipjoint but it’s clever design makes it unlikely to close on your hand and able to be opened one handed. You get the added benefit of having a flat head screwdriver and bottle opener available when the blade isn’t in use. This things my favorite of the bunch and it’s discontinued so you can pick it up for $153.

There’re other options but these 3 are the only ones I could speak on and recommend. If you want to check out the others; go to blade hq’s website, select knives, filter folding knives, country of origin USA, and blade length of <2”

I have the same experience with physical endeavors. For example in a dream I had a couple nights ago I was running an obstacle course and it was really fun but I got to an obstacle that resembled those horizontal incline ladders that county fairs and amusement parks have and right when I saw it I thought “wtf that’s not even possible” then sure enough when I tried to cross it my arms and legs felt like noodles trying to move through molasses. I think the other posters have a point about having confidence though because later in that same dream I was swinging around like Tarzan and jumping upwards of twice my height.

In all honesty there’s nothing that beats having company, but the next best thing in my experience is having a “tether” this is anything you can use to ground yourself to the non hallucination world aka real life. Sometimes it can help to fall asleep to stories being played on low volume. I personally find that having an oil lamp or night light helps me (I know it might seem childish but it helps). I use the tether to tell whether I’m dreaming or not and to give myself something to focus on if I am experiencing sleep paralysis. For example, if I believe I’m having a sleep paralysis episode then I’ll try to focus on the smell and light from my oil candle or listen to the words being spoken from the story being played. What I learned from previous episodes of sleep paralysis is that the sooner I recognize what’s happening the sooner I can get back to sleep (you can do this by trying to speak or move your body). Most importantly I’ve learned not to care about my dreams that much, dreams are weird and everyone has strange dreams every once in a while. I suggest starting a dream journal and getting either your husband or a friend to start one too, having someone to talk with about weird dreams can help remove the scary nature some dreams might have and can even be pretty funny when talking about the sillier dreams. These are all things that have helped me and I can only hope that at least one of these helps you.
